title: Jump Game
corePattern: Greedy Reachability Tracking - Farthest Reachable Index
interviewTips: Clarify constraints: can you assume non-negative integers? Is single element [0] considered already at last index (true)?

Trade-off to discuss: Brute force explores all jump combinations O(2^n) vs DP memoizes O(n^2) vs Greedy tracks max reach in O(n) with O(1) space - explain why greedy is safe because order does not matter, only farthest reach.
Edge-case tip: mention early exit when i > maxReach, zeros that trap you e.g., [3,2,1,0,4], and large jumps that overshoot end; test [0], [2,0,0] and [1,0,1,0].

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Backtracking
approaches.intuition: From each index i try every possible jump 1..nums[i] recursively. If any path reaches the end, answer is true. This is depth-first search over all jump choices.
approaches.theory: Model positions as nodes and jumps as directed edges i -> j for i<j<=i+nums[i]. The question is whether n-1 is reachable from 0. Brute force DFS explores all paths without memoization, so overlapping subproblems are recomputed exponentially. Correct but only for understanding baseline.

timeComplexity.explanation: In worst case each position branches up to nums[i] ways, leading to exponential number of paths. E.g., nums = [4,4,4,...] explores ~2^n calls.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Recursion stack depth up to n in worst case chain of jumps of length 1.

steps: dfs(0): can jump to 1,2 -> try dfs(1)
dfs(1): can jump to 2,3,4 -> try dfs(2)
dfs(2): can jump to 3 -> try dfs(3)
dfs(3): can jump to 4 -> try dfs(4)
dfs(4): i >= n-1 -> return True, unwinds to True

edgeCases: Zero in middle e.g., [2,0,0] -> true via direct jump over zeros

approaches.name: Approach 2: Top-Down DP with Memoization
approaches.intuition: Many positions are revisited by brute force. Cache result for each index as GOOD (can reach end), BAD (cannot), or UNKNOWN. Compute once per index.
approaches.theory: Define dp[i] = whether suffix starting at i can reach end. Recurrence: dp[n-1]=True, dp[i]= OR_{j in (i+1..i+nums[i])} dp[j]. Compute via DFS + memo top-down or bottom-up right-to-left. Memoization prunes repeated work from exponential to polynomial because each i is expanded at most once over its outgoing edges.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each index i is visited once and scans up to nums[i] <= n successors, so total O(n^2) worst case.

spaceComplexity.explanation: O(n) memo array plus O(n) recursion stack.

steps: dfs(1) tries 2,3; dfs(2) tries 3; dfs(3) has nums[3]=0, no moves -> BAD
dfs(2) only leads to BAD -> BAD, dfs(1) only leads to BAD -> BAD

edgeCases: [2,0,0] -> dfs(1) is BAD but dfs(0) jumps directly to 2 GOOD -> true
Long array of 1s [1,1,1,...,1] -> O(n^2) but still passes, chain of GOOD

approaches.name: Approach 3: Greedy Max Reach (Optimal)
approaches.intuition: We do not need to know exact jump path, only how far we can reach so far. Sweep left to right maintaining maxReach = max(maxReach, i+nums[i]). If current i is beyond maxReach, there is a gap and we are stuck.
approaches.theory: Greedy invariant: after processing indices < i, maxReach is the farthest index reachable using any jumps from [0,i-1]. If i > maxReach, i is unreachable -> return false. Otherwise we can extend maxReach with i. If maxReach >= n-1 at any point, return true. This is correct because reachability is monotone: being able to reach farther can only help, never hurt. Equivalent to backward greedy tracking last good position.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single linear pass, constant work per index.

edgeCases: Single element [0] -> loop i=0 maxReach>=0 -> true
[3,2,1,0,4]: i=0 maxReach=3, i=1 maxReach=3, i=2 maxReach=3, i=3 maxReach=3, i=4 4>3 -> false
[2,0,0]: i=0 maxReach=2 >=2 -> true without visiting gap
